prose_changes.old: In the early 1870s a young Pittsburgh clothing merchant named Charles Taze Russell gathered a small circle to study the Bible without reference to inherited denominational teaching, and in 1879 began a magazine, Zion's Watch Tower and Herald of Christ's Presence. Around the magazine grew an international network of readers who called themselves Bible Students, distributed Russell's six-volume Studies in the Scriptures by the million, worked door to door as colporteurs, and gathered for annual conventions from 1893. The movement was built on printing and personal distribution from the very start, which is why its record of itself is unusually complete for a body of its size. The name Jehovah's Witnesses, and the tightly centralized organization the movement is known for today, came later — after Russell's death in 1916, under his successor Joseph Franklin Rutherford.
prose_changes.new: In the early 1870s Charles Taze Russell, a young clothing merchant in Pittsburgh, gathered a small circle to study the Bible. They aimed to read it for themselves, free of the teaching handed down by the churches. In 1879 Russell began a magazine, Zion's Watch Tower and Herald of Christ's Presence. A network of readers in many countries grew up around it. They called themselves Bible Students. They handed out Russell's six-volume Studies in the Scriptures by the million. They went door to door as colporteurs, traveling sellers of religious books. From 1893 they met each year at large conventions. The movement was built on print and on handing books from person to person from the very start. That is why its record of itself is so full for a body of its size. The name Jehovah's Witnesses came later, and so did the tightly run central body the movement is known for today. Both came after Russell's death in 1916, under his successor, Joseph Franklin Rutherford.
prose_changes.reason: 'Without reference to inherited denominational teaching' stated the circle's aim as fact; the movement's cited scholars (Penton; Chryssides) show Russell drawing on Adventist preachers. Now an aim. Every other fact kept; long sentences split to meet the reading target, and 'colporteurs' explained.

The name Jehovah's Witnesses and the centralized organization it is known for today came only after Russell's death in 1916.

They aimed to read it free of the teaching handed down by the churches. In 1879 he began the magazine that grew into a network of Bible Students in many countries. Twentieth-century court and tribunal reports (US Jehovah's Witnesses cases; Christian Science child-treatment cases; British and US objector tribunals) would test the legacy claims; most fall after the era and may not be public domain.
escalations: Not urgent, for Mark: none of the four texts names another movement on the map, so this group drafts no links. Three well-attested ties go unnamed: John Thomas's years in the Stone-Campbell movement and his break with Alexander Campbell; Russell's debt to Adventist preachers (Wendell, Storrs, Barbour); and Eddy's 1862 treatment by Phineas Quimby, whose role is disputed. Each would be a cross-part link to a part-1 movement or to Spiritualism / New Thought. Adding them means adding text, so it is a cross-world decision, not a drafter's.
